messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Miriam Holloway is a 76-year-old divorced woman who has served on her city's council for over a decade, a role that has long given her a sense of order and civic purpose that her childhood home never offered. She came to the current intake with a PCL-5 score of 48, describing a presentation that, in her own words, she had "managed to outrun for most of my life" — until recently, she no longer could.

The trauma Miriam witnessed unfolded across years rather than in a single incident, but the most formative episode occurred when she was nine years old. She describes standing in the hallway of the family home, frozen, as her father — a large man who smelled of cigarettes and something medicinal — pinned her mother against the kitchen wall during a medical crisis her mother had tried to manage quietly at home. A visiting nurse had arrived to examine her mother, and Miriam watched as her father's rage at the intrusion became physical. The nurse's latex gloves, the clinical smell of antiseptic, her mother's suppressed cry, and the particular way her father's voice dropped before he struck — these details lodged somewhere that decades of adult competence could not fully reach. Comments from extended family in the years that followed — "your father had his reasons," "don't air what happens at home" — taught Miriam early that the event was unspeakable, and she became expert at not speaking it, even to herself.

What brings her to treatment now is a convergence of exposures she can no longer avoid. As a council member, Miriam attends community health forums and ribbon-cuttings at medical facilities. In recent months, the smell of antiseptic in a hospital corridor during a site visit, or the sight of a nurse snapping on latex gloves, has been enough to collapse the distance she has maintained for sixty-seven years. These moments function as potent triggers precisely because they replicate the sensory texture of that hallway: the medicinal smell, the clinical instruments, the atmosphere of examination and helplessness. When triggered in this way, she does not always retrieve a coherent image — sometimes what arrives is only the emotion, raw and sourceless, a wave of dread and shame with no picture attached, as though the feeling has survived the memory intact. At other times the memory feels more present and vivid than anything happening in the room around her, more real than the council chamber or the faces of her colleagues — the past momentarily outweighing the present in sensory weight.

This quality of the memory, in turn, makes her more vigilant in her daily environment. Because the recollection can arrive so suddenly and feel so immediate, Miriam has become hyperattentive to anything that might summon it. She scans for her estranged father — now in his late nineties and occasionally mentioned by relatives — at family-adjacent civic events, and the mere possibility of seeing him at a community gathering has caused her to pre-emptively decline two public appearances this year. Comments about family, whether offered casually by a constituent or raised in a council discussion about domestic policy, land on her with a force disproportionate to their intent; each one becomes a potential trigger, and she has learned to steer conversations away from them with the practiced efficiency of someone who has been doing so for most of her adult life.

She has also begun pushing the memories away before they can fully form — a habit she describes as necessary but exhausting, like pressing a hand over a wound. She is aware, dimly, that this effort prevents her from knowing exactly what she is afraid of, but she has come to believe that full recall would be worse than the partial images she currently endures.

What finally brought Miriam to seek help was a scheduled cardiac examination — routine, her physician assured her — that she postponed three times before admitting she could not enter the clinic without shaking. She is most afraid, she says, that after seventy-six years of managing this alone, she will not be able to stop it from undoing the professional life she has built. What she is hoping for, quietly, is simply to be able to walk into a medical office without her childhood following her through the door.
